Vieillir en famille: un choix de société: Aging in Family: A Societal Choice
« Si je tombe malade et que je deviens l: “If I get sick and become a vegetable, let me go. Don’t put me in a home.”
Les spécialistes en gériatrie recommande: Geriatric specialists increasingly recommend that seniors age alongside their families, with help from the state if necessary. But Enice Toussaint and Jean-Paul Langlois didn’t need experts to tell them so: their lived experience speaks for itself. There’s always something going on at the Toussaints’. Enice, 74, lives with her brother and her grandchildren in a small house on the Plateau Mont-Royal, left to her by her older sister. A nurse by trade, her sister spent her retirement volunteering in CHSLDs, and Enice will never forget what her sister used to tell her: “If I get sick and become a vegetable, let me go. Don’t put me in a home.”
Il faut dire que l’entraide familiale fa: Mutual support within the family is part of the mindset and values of the Haitian community, she says. “It’s rare for us to put our parents in a CHSLD. Even if someone has Alzheimer’s, we take care of them. Relatives and friends come to help,” explains the septuagenarian. Her granddaughter, Elle Camay, knows how lucky she is. “There’s a wisdom that comes from living day to day with your grandmother or an uncle. You learn from their life experience and their precious advice,” says the 24-year-old literature student. In the evening, the young adults close their bedroom doors and turn the volume down. During the day, they help carry the grocery bags. The clan is tight-knit. For Elle Camay, this model is ideal. Her words are enough to reassure Enice. Her dearest wish is to grow old for as long as possible in the company of her loved ones. She thinks of a blind woman in the neighbourhood who, at 97, still lives with her 70-year-old son. “We have to keep seniors at home for as long as possible. Let them be in peace in their own homes, and let’s find people to help them day to day,” she believes.
Le coronavirus rappelle à Jean-Paul Lang: The coronavirus reminds Jean-Paul Langlois of his childhood in the 1940s in Sainte-Flore, in the Mauricie region. His grandfather lived across from his family, on the other side of the rural road. Overnight, visits were forbidden. Tuberculosis was spreading terror everywhere. He and his family watched helplessly as three of his aunts died, aged 23, 27 and 29. The 84-year-old recalls these memories from his luxury high-rise residence in Longueuil. Inside, tenants have access to a swimming pool, a billiard table, a balcony and a large underground garage.
Mais Jean-Paul n’hésiterait pas à troque: But Jean-Paul wouldn’t hesitate to trade this comfort for life with family. He is, in fact, nurturing a lovely project with his daughter Lorraine: building a multigenerational house in Longueuil. “We’re following the example of my sister Monique, who sold her house in Shawinigan to go live with her daughter and her two grandchildren,” he says. In the meantime, Jean-Paul is being patient and keeping busy with personal projects. “I feel a bit like a prisoner,” he confides. “If only I could have driven a little, just to get a change of air.” He consoles himself by thinking of his friend, a former work colleague who lives in a similar tower in Montréal. She stays confined to her room all day long. “At least I can go downstairs to get my mail. And my daughters come to see me. Through the glass, we can talk on the phone.”
Les vœux de Jean-Paul et d’Enice sont pa: Jean-Paul’s and Enice’s wishes are shared by a growing number of experts. Premier François Legault himself has spoken of a social reflection that needs to be considered. “Our parents and grandparents end up in CHSLDs more than anywhere else in the world,” he said recently. Gina Bravo, a researcher at the Research Centre on Aging in Sherbrooke, fears other pandemics to come. She believes we must begin by moving away from the current model, which favours housing seniors in residences or CHSLDs. “Some elderly people stopped eating. Some died without their families even knowing. As a society, this shows a failure.”
Le modèle actuel ne fonctionne pas, dit: The current model isn’t working, says Catherine Dorion of Québec Solidaire, who goes so far as to suggest abolishing CHSLDs. Over the past few years, the public was informed by the Auditor General’s investigation reports or by cries from the heart sent out by caregivers. “It was scandalous, much like today, and then afterwards, we forgot about it,” analyzes the 37-year-old politician. Her party suggests allowances that would work the same way as the Quebec Parental Insurance Plan (QPIP). “That would allow a family caregiver to hire people for basic care and take a break.” A spot in a CHSLD costs $100,000 a year. “You can get a lot of mileage out of $100,000,” says Catherine Dorion. “Why doesn’t the government put that money into home care?” Many claim that we have abandoned our seniors. That we “parked” them there. “That’s not entirely true,” believes Ms. Dorion. “It has become individual choices that are part of our culture. It’s sad. At the same time, it’s easy to tell someone: take care of your father who has Alzheimer’s. Where is he going to get the money? He has to stop working. We don’t live in a community where people help each other,” she laments. Ms. Dorion suggests drawing inspiration from Denmark or the Netherlands, which devote more than 70% of their public spending to home care.
Au Québec, cette statistique s’élève à s: In Quebec, that figure is only 15%. Should we draw inspiration from European countries like Switzerland and Austria, which offer financial allowances to those who take care of their parents? Is Quebec society ready to follow the model of Enice Toussaint, who lives happily with her grandchildren? “It’s a big bus that has to be turned around, and that’s not easy,” concludes geriatrics researcher Gina Bravo.
